content: 1. Advise the mother to breastfeed more frequently and reassess after two feeds (approximately one day). If there is no improvement, teach the mother how to express enough breast milk before feeding to relieve discomfort. 2. If part of the breast is painful, swollen, and red, and the mother has a temperature above 38°C, this indicates mastitis. Encourage the mother to continue breastfeeding and teach her correct positioning and attachment. Prescribe cloxacillin for 10 days and reassess in two days. If there is no improvement or the condition worsens, refer the mother to a hospital. 3. If the mother is HIV-infected, advise her to breastfeed on the healthy breast and express milk from the affected breast, discarding it until there is no fever. If the pain is severe, administer paracetamol. 4. If the breasts are healthy (no swelling, redness, tenderness, soreness, or fissures, and the body temperature is normal), reassure the mother. 5. Ensure the room is warm (not less than 25°C and free of drafts). Keep the baby in the room with the mother, either in her bed or within easy reach. If the baby is in a cot, ensure they are dressed, wrapped, and covered with a blanket, including a hat for the head. 6. Support exclusive breastfeeding on demand, day and night. Ask the mother to alert you if she experiences breastfeeding difficulties. Assess breastfeeding in every baby before discharge. 7. Teach the mother how to care for the baby, including keeping the baby warm, providing cord care, and ensuring hygiene. Do not expose the baby to direct sunlight or place them on cold surfaces. 8. If the mother is unable to care for the baby, provide care or teach a companion. Wash hands before and after handling the baby. Ask the mother or companion to monitor the baby and alert you if the baby’s feet are cold or if there are breathing difficulties (grunting, fast or slow breathing, chest in-drawing). 9. If the baby’s feet are cold, teach the mother to use skin-to-skin contact to warm the baby and reassess in one hour. If the feet remain cold, measure the temperature and rewarm the baby. 10. If there is bleeding from the umbilical cord, check if the tie is loose and retie it. For other bleeding, assess the baby immediately. 11. If there are breathing difficulties or any other abnormalities reported by the mother, examine the baby thoroughly. Administer prescribed treatments as per the schedule and examine the baby before planning discharge. Do not discharge the baby before they are 24 hours old. 12. For small babies (preterm or weighing 1500g to <2500g), plan to keep them longer before discharge. Provide special breastfeeding support, encourage feeding every 2-3 hours, and assess breastfeeding daily. If the baby is not sucking effectively and has no other danger signs, consider alternative feeding methods. 13. Teach the mother how to hand express breast milk directly into the baby’s mouth or use cup feeding. Determine the appropriate daily milk amount based on the baby’s age. If feeding difficulties persist for three days or weight loss exceeds 10% of birth weight, refer for breastfeeding counseling and management. 14. Ensure additional warmth for small babies by maintaining a room temperature of 25–28°C, teaching the mother skin-to-skin contact, and providing extra blankets. Do not bathe the small baby; wash as needed. 15. For very small babies (<1500g or >2 months early), refer urgently to the hospital, ensuring extra warmth during referral. For small babies (1500g–<2500g or 32–36 weeks), provide kangaroo mother care, special breastfeeding support, and reassess daily. Do not discharge until the baby is feeding well, gaining weight, and has stable body temperature. 16. For twins, provide special breastfeeding support and do not discharge until both twins are ready to go home. 17. Assess breastfeeding in every baby as part of the examination. If the mother reports nipple or breast pain, assess her breasts as well. Observe breastfeeding for about five minutes if the baby has not fed in the previous hour. 18. Look for proper attachment, positioning, and effective sucking. If the baby is not sucking effectively after six hours of age, refer urgently to the hospital. Ensure the baby is breastfeeding at least eight times in 24 hours and not receiving other foods or drinks. 19. Support exclusive breastfeeding, teach correct positioning and attachment, and advise the mother to feed more frequently, day and night. Reassure her that she has enough milk and advise against feeding the baby other foods or drinks. Reassess at the next feed or follow-up visit in two days. 20. For babies with feeding difficulties, teach the mother replacement feeding and cup feeding. Advise feeding more frequently on demand, day and night, and stop feeding the baby other foods or drinks. Reassess at the next feed or follow-up visit in two days. 21. For babies at risk of bacterial infection, administer two intramuscular antibiotics for five days and assess the baby daily. For risk of congenital syphilis, give a single dose of benzathine penicillin and ensure the mother and partner are treated. 22. For babies at risk of HIV transmission, administer antiretroviral (ARV) therapy to the newborn and teach the mother how to give ARVs. Counsel on infant feeding options and provide special counseling for breastfeeding mothers. 23. For babies at risk of tuberculosis, provide isoniazid prophylaxis for six months and administer the BCG vaccine only after completing treatment. Follow up in two weeks. 24. If the baby has severe jaundice (yellow skin on the face and less than 24 hours old), refer urgently to the hospital. Encourage breastfeeding on the way, and if there are feeding difficulties, provide expressed breast milk by cup. 25. Always examine the baby in the presence of the mother. Check for danger signs such as preterm birth, difficult birth, resuscitation at birth, convulsions, or frequent vomiting. Assess breathing, movements, skin, umbilicus, and temperature. If the baby is cold or very warm, measure the temperature and take appropriate action. 26. For well babies (normal weight, feeding effectively eight times in 24 hours, no danger signs, and no special treatment needs), provide breastfeeding counseling, administer vitamin K, and ensure care for the newborn. Examine again before discharge and provide immunizations if due. Advise on routine postnatal contacts and when to return if danger signs appear. Record findings in the home-based record.
